frontmatter.title: 9. Physiology
frontmatter.subtitle: Physiology and measurement of bodily responses to music

children.value: This week follows on from the previous week’s focus on music-related movement and embodiment, investigating the body’s measurable physiological responses to sound and music: heart rate and heart-rate variability, skin conductance, respiration, and muscle tension, the autonomic mechanisms behind them, and the problems of measuring these signals in the lab, at concerts, or with wearables.
(knowledge) term with physio- coming from the Greek

, meaning nature or natural processes. So physiology literally means “the study of nature”. In modern biology it refers to the study of how living organisms and their parts function: how the heart, the lungs, the skin, and the nervous system do their jobs and keep the body in balance. For this course, we will focus on how music changes what the body does, in performers and perceivers.
Have you experienced any physiological reactions to music?
Most of the signals in this chapter are run by the
, the part of the nervous system that works without being asked. It has two branches with opposite jobs. The
prepares the body for action: it raises heart rate and blood pressure, increases sweating, and sends blood to the muscles. The
, does the opposite: it slows the heart, aids digestion, and supports rest and recovery.

The two branches work at different speeds. The parasympathetic branch can change the heart rate within a single beat; sympathetic effects build up over seconds to minutes. That difference matters whenever you try to line up a bodily response with the musical event that caused it.

Playing music is physical work and social exposure at once, and a performer’s body shows both. Typically, heart rate rises and its beat-to-beat variability (HRV) falls in passages that are exciting, loud, or physically demanding, and the reverse happens in calm, slow ones. In choirs and ensembles the performers’ heart rhythms often become more alike, the more so the better they know the piece and each other.

Breathing follows the music most closely of all, which is why it is one of the most relevant signals to record from singers and wind players. Phrases set where a breath can be taken and tempo sets how long it can last. All types of performers often also use breath as a cue: an audible intake before an entry tells the others when to come in, so a respiration recording shows both one performer’s strategy and the group’s coordination.
, a steady pulse can draw breathing and heart rhythm into step with it through an entrainment process. The tension and release of

can show up as rises and falls in arousal. How strongly any of this happens depends on the performer: training, fitness, familiarity with the piece, nerves, and the role in the ensemble all change both the size and the direction of what is measured.
Dig deeper: entrainment across physiological timescales

as coupled oscillators falling into a stable phase relationship, and applied there to attention and movement. What is new here is which oscillator is doing the coupling. In physiology, bodily rhythms—neural oscillations, respiration, heart rate, motor activity—come to track an external auditory pulse, or each other, through sensorimotor coupling and autonomic adjustment. The observable effects are respiratory and cardiac phase alignment to tempo, and neural phase-locking to rhythmic structure.

The practical consequence is a spread of timescales that the musical case does not have. Entrainment here runs from millisecond neural synchrony through second-scale breathing changes to minute-scale autonomic shifts, so the lag between a musical event and its physiological trace depends on which signal you are recording. Strength still depends on the same factors as before: stimulus salience, attention, and motor involvement, plus the individual’s baseline rhythms.
Beyond autonomic timing, musical engagement evokes neurochemical and hormonal responses that shape affect and social bonding.
changes tied to stress or performance anxiety can all accompany strong musical experiences and modulate the size and persistence of physiological synchrony.

Even though perceivers are “passive” compared to the performers, they too have physiological reactions to music. Slow, soft music with smooth, dark timbres tends to calm the body: heart rate falls, its variability rises, and the skin sweats less. Fast, loud music with sharp attacks and bright timbres does the opposite. There are cultural and individual differences, but music heard as pleasant and relaxing generally calms, while music heard as suspenseful or threatening activates.
(HRV) are often negatively correlated. As HR rises, HRV commonly falls, because shorter interbeat intervals mechanically limit beat-to-beat variability.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

# A simulated three-minute recording of heartbeats. Heart rate climbs from rest to arousal, and the
# beat-to-beat variability shrinks as it does: the breathing-linked swing of the intervals gets smaller
# when the parasympathetic branch withdraws, and shorter intervals leave less room to vary in any case.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
t, rr, times = 0.0, [], []
while t < 180:
    phase = min(1.0, max(0.0, (t - 60) / 90))              # rest for a minute, then a 90 s rise, then a plateau
    hr = 62 + 40 * phase                                     # beats per minute
    mean_rr = 60 / hr                                        # seconds
    rsa = (0.09 - 0.07 * phase) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 4.5)  # breathing-linked swing, 4.5 s per breath
    noise = (0.025 - 0.018 * phase) * rng.standard_normal()
    interval = max(0.3, mean_rr + rsa * mean_rr + noise)
    times.append(t); rr.append(interval); t += interval
times, rr = np.array(times), np.array(rr) * 1000             # ms

# heart rate and RMSSD in 30 s windows
edges = np.arange(0, 181, 30); hr_w, hrv_w = [], []
for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    sel = (times >= a) & (times < b); ibi = rr[sel]
    hr_w.append(60000 / ibi.mean()); hrv_w.append(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.diff(ibi) ** 2)))

# the heartbeat signal itself, drawn as an idealised ECG on the simulated beat times
def ecg(beat_times, t0, t1, fs=500):
    tt = np.arange(t0, t1, 1 / fs); y = np.zeros_like(tt)
    for b in beat_times[(beat_times > t0 - 1) & (beat_times < t1 + 1)]:
        for centre, width, height in [(-0.16, 0.025, 0.15), (-0.025, 0.008, -0.10), (0.0, 0.010, 1.0), (0.025, 0.008, -0.25), (0.30, 0.050, 0.30)]:
            y += height * np.exp(-((tt - b - centre) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2))
    return tt, y

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1, 1.3], width_ratios=[1.6, 1], hspace=0.5, wspace=0.45)
for col, (t0, label) in enumerate([(20, "at rest"), (160, "aroused")]):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, col]); tt, y = ecg(times, t0, t0 + 5)
    ax.plot(tt - t0, y, color="C0", lw=1.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.85); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False); ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
    beats = times[(times >= t0) & (times < t0 + 5)]
    for k, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(beats[:-1], beats[1:])):
        yy = 1.25 if k % 2 == 0 else 1.5                     # alternate heights so close labels do not collide
        ax.annotate("", (b - t0, yy), (a - t0, yy), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="0.4", lw=1))
        ax.text((a + b) / 2 - t0, yy + 0.05, f"{(b - a) * 1000:.0f} ms", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color="0.3")
    sel = (times >= t0) & (times < t0 + 30)
    ax.set_title(f"Five seconds {label}: about {60000 / rr[sel].mean():.0f} beats per minute")
ax0 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0]); ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])
ax0.plot(times, rr, color="C0", lw=1)
ax0.set_xlabel("Time (s)"); ax0.set_ylabel("Interval between beats (ms)")
ax0.set_title("Beats get closer, and their swing shrinks")
sec = ax0.secondary_yaxis("right", functions=(lambda ms: 60000 / ms, lambda bpm: 60000 / bpm))   # the same axis in beats per minute
sec.set_ylabel("Heart rate (bpm)")
ax0.axvspan(0, 60, color="0.92", lw=0); ax0.text(30, ax0.get_ylim()[1] * 0.98, "rest", ha="center", va="top", color="0.4")
ax0.text(150, ax0.get_ylim()[1] * 0.98, "aroused", ha="center", va="top", color="0.4")
ax1.plot(hr_w, hrv_w, "o-", color="C1")
for k, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(hr_w, hrv_w)):
    ax1.annotate(f"{int(edges[k])}–{int(edges[k+1])} s", (x, y), xytext=(5, 3), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color="0.3")
ax1.set_xlabel("Heart rate (bpm)"); ax1.set_ylabel("Variability, RMSSD (ms)")
ax1.set_title("Higher rate, lower variability")
plt.show()

children.value: Figure: A simulated three-minute recording in which heart rate climbs from rest to arousal. Top: five seconds of the heartbeat signal at rest and five seconds aroused, with the gap between successive beats marked; at a higher heart rate the beats come closer, so each interval is shorter. Bottom left: the interval between beats over the whole recording, shortening as the rate climbs, with the breathing-linked swing of the intervals shrinking too. Bottom right: heart rate against heart-rate variability (RMSSD) in 30-second windows of the same recording: as one rises, the other falls. Real recordings are noisier, but the direction is the same, which is why the two should never be read apart.
A steady, slow pulse can slow a perceiver’s breathing, and with it the heart, which speeds up slightly on each in-breath and slows on the out-breath (

); faster music does the reverse. How much any one perceiver responds depends on baseline, training, familiarity, culture, mood, and attention, and on the setting: people listening together in a hall respond more, and more alike, than people listening alone.
Advances in measurement now allow empirical study of

physiological responses to music. As noted above, music can bring bodies into sync, both in performance and in perception. A common beat can make people breathe together, and once breathing is shared, heart rate, skin conductance and even brain activity can start to look more similar across perceivers or performers.
A few simple routes lead here. Sensorimotor entrainment (
) means that moving, tapping or dancing together aligns bodily rhythms.
describes how emotion spreads through a group and shifts autonomic signals like heart rate and skin conductance.
and hormonal responses—for example feeling connected or safe, sometimes linked to
We measure such interpersonal responses by looking for moment-to-moment similarity between signals such as heart rate and respiration. Common tools are
(checking whether two signals rise and fall together, possibly with a delay), windowed
or windowed correlation (testing similarity in short time windows to see when coupling appears), and
(checking whether rhythmic signals keep a stable phase relationship). Because these signals run continuously, a good analysis says
people are coordinated, not only whether they are on average;
developed such an activity analysis for continuous responses to music.
In a RITMO study of expert and student string quartets, the players’ cardiac rhythms became more interrelated in passages of shared musical absorption

. In another study, MusicLab Copenhagen, the Danish String Quartet performed to both on-site and remove audiences. It was found that the audience in the hall felt more connected to each other than the streaming audience did

. Interestingly, both felt equally connected to the performers, and the hall audience moved less during the classical pieces and more during the folk tunes. Coupling tends to be stronger when people interact directly, attend to the same thing, or are emotionally engaged with the music.

The signals described so far rarely appear on their own. A rising heart rate or a burst of sweat usually accompanies an emotional experience, so it is worth pausing to ask what an emotion actually is. In psychology, an

is a relatively brief, intense reaction to something that matters to us, combining a subjective feeling, bodily changes, and often an urge to act. Hearing a sudden bang behind you, for example, joins the feeling of alarm to a racing heart and an impulse to duck.
Emotions should not be confused with

, which last longer and are less clearly tied to a specific cause. An emotion is short, from seconds to minutes, while a mood lasts hours or days. An emotion is about something (a sudden chord or a face in the audience), while a mood has no clear object and colours whatever comes along. And an emotion is intense enough to change the body and prompt an action, while a mood is a lower, steadier background. Music works on both: a piece can induce an emotion at one moment but also shift a mood for the afternoon.

The difference between emotion and mood matters for how they are measured. An emotion shows up in a physiological recording as a brief, phasic response time-locked to the moment that caused it; a mood shows up, if at all, as a slow change in the tonic level over the session, which is why it is so important to measure baseline values.
There is one more important thing to think of: the distinction between

. Perceived emotion is what you recognise the music as expressing. Induced (or felt) emotion is what the music makes you feel. Most people would recognise a sad emotion in a ballad in minor. But it does not necessarily make you sad yourself. In fact, many people instead report feeling moved, comforted, or pleasantly melancholic. The two often overlap, but they can come apart, and every study of musical emotion has to state which of them it is measuring.

Emotions can be described with categories (happy, sad, angry, tender) or with dimensions. The most widely used dimensional model in music research is the circumplex model of affect, also called the valence–arousal model, proposed by the American psychologist
. It arranges emotional states in a circle around two axes: valence, running from unpleasant to pleasant, and arousal, running from calm to activated (see
). Happiness is pleasant and activated, sadness unpleasant and calm, anger unpleasant and activated, and relaxation pleasant and calm.

The model is popular because two numbers are enough to place a track, or a single moment within it, on a map. The figure below shows one possible placement of some well-known tracks. Your own placements would differ, which is itself a finding, since the map describes responses rather than properties of the audio file.

A map says where an emotion sits, not how the music got you there. The Swedish music psychologist Patrik Juslin has argued that musical emotions arise through a set of underlying psychological mechanisms, each of which also operates outside music
. The main ones are worth knowing:
: Sudden, loud, or sharp events trigger the body’s fast alarm circuits. A gunshot-like drum hit, or the drop in an EDM track, startles the body before any thinking has happened.
: Bodily rhythms lock onto a strong external pulse, as in the choir case above. A steady four-on-the-floor beat can wind arousal up over several minutes on a dance floor.
: A piece heard repeatedly in happy settings eventually triggers the happiness by itself, a musical form of
. The chime of an ice-cream van can still cheer up an adult decades later.

: We catch the emotion the music expresses, much as emotion spreads between people (see the interpersonal section above). A voice cracking with grief in a ballad can pull the perceiver’s own state along with it.
, and the emotion follows the image. A slowly swelling synthesiser pad may evoke a sunrise, together with the calm that belongs to it.
reawakens the feelings of that moment, which is why couples speak of “our song”.
: Music sets up predictions and then confirms, delays, or violates them, and those prediction errors are felt as tension, surprise, and release

Several mechanisms can run at once, and different mechanisms dominate for different perceivers and situations. That is one reason the same song can give one person chills and leave another cold. The list also explains why perceived and induced emotion can part ways. You can recognise the grief in a ballad through contagion without feeling it yourself, or feel a surge of joy from an episodic memory attached to a song that expresses nothing joyful at all.
Think of a song that makes you feel something different from what it expresses. Which of the mechanisms above might explain the mismatch?
Sad music is the classic test case for these mechanisms. Jonna Vuoskoski and Tuomas Eerola showed with indirect measures that sad music induces genuine sadness rather than only a recognition of it
, and that the people who enjoy sad music tend to score high on empathy and openness to experience

. Why anyone should enjoy feeling sad is the puzzle, and their later study resolved it: the pleasure that sad music gives is carried not by the sadness but by the feeling of being moved, which rises with the sadness and is what listeners come back for
. Empathy also predicts how strongly a perceiver catches the emotion that music expresses, which is one reason the contagion mechanism varies so much from person to person.

Measuring an emotion is harder than measuring a heartbeat. The most direct tool is self-report: asking perceivers to rate valence and arousal, pick emotion words, or move a slider while the music plays. Self-report reaches the felt experience, but it depends on memory and vocabulary, and continuous rating is itself a task that changes the listening. The physiological signals covered in the next section offer a complement, since they run continuously, do not interrupt the music, and cannot be embellished afterwards. Their weakness is the opposite one. No single signal maps neatly onto an emotion, because a racing heart can mean joy, fear, or a flight of stairs. Careful studies therefore combine both kinds of measure, and state clearly whether participants report what the music expresses or what they themselves feel.
Dig deeper: which emotion model to use

Which emotion words or dimensions to offer is itself a research question. A comparison of the discrete model (happy, sad, tender, fearful, angry) with the dimensional one (valence, arousal) on the same film music excerpts found both workable, with the dimensional model coping better with ambiguous examples

. Continuous ratings add the time dimension. When several hundred perceivers rated moment by moment how moved they felt, the experience showed the same pattern of appraisals and bodily sensations as being moved by social scenes in film, which supports the view of feeling moved as a social emotion

Such measurements can also leave the lab. In our collaboration with the Stavanger Symphony Orchestra, we have brought these methods into school concerts, recording performers’ heart rate and respiration during full orchestral pieces. As part of this work we have also experimented with an emotion visualiser, turning audience responses into graphics that can be shown and discussed with the pupils. The invisible link between music and feeling then becomes something a school class can see and argue about.
Strong musical emotions sometimes come with an unmistakable bodily signature, and one of them has received particular attention.
Interest has grown in recent years in musical chills (

), brief peak-emotional responses often reported as goosebumps, shivers, or a cold sensation along the spine. These events come with transient autonomic signatures such as brief rises in skin conductance, short-lived heart-rate and respiration changes, pupil dilation and visible piloerection (hair standing on end), and neuroimaging work links them to reward circuits (e.g., the nucleus accumbens). The pupil response is large enough to serve as a marker: in a study at the University of Oslo, perceivers’ pupils dilated at the moments in the music where they reported chills, most strongly for music they had chosen themselves

. Chills are typically triggered by salient musical features—unexpected harmonic shifts, climactic crescendos, intimate vocal timbres, or passages tied to personal memories—and they vary widely across perceivers depending on personality, familiarity, context and attention. Note how these triggers echo the mechanisms above, with expectancy, episodic memory, and contagion doing much of the work.
Do you experience chills when listening to music? Are there any particular songs or musical features that more easily evoke chills?

Identify one passage of music that reliably gives you chills. Describe, in a short paragraph each: what happens in the music at that exact moment (harmony, dynamics, timbre, texture, entry of a voice), what you notice in your body, and how you would design a study to test whether your explanation is right for perceivers other than you.

(ASMR) is another phenomenon that has drawn attention in recent years. It refers to a set of pleasurable, often tingling sensations and deep relaxation brought on by soft, intimate auditory and multimodal cues—whispering, close-mic breathing, gentle tapping, slow movements and binaural spatialisation—that overlap with some musical timbral and production techniques. The video below,
ASMR For People Who Don’t Get Tingles
by the creator Jojo’s ASMR, demonstrates several of these triggers:
(If the video is unavailable, try the

In sound and music research, ASMR is relevant because its triggers show how micro-acoustic features (low-level dynamics, spectral detail, and spatial cues) and a sense of interpersonal closeness modulate autonomic state. Many perceivers report calming, parasympathetic effects (slower breathing, lowered heart rate) alongside transient markers such as piloerection and occasional phasic skin-conductance rises.

ASMR and frisson can co-occur, but they differ phenomenologically and physiologically. ASMR is typically soothing and prolonged, whereas frisson is brief and strongly reward-linked. Analyses should therefore treat them as distinct response classes and include timing, valence and arousal measures to tell their profiles apart.
Many physiological signals can be recorded. Here we look at some of the more common ones used in music research.
There are two main ways to measure heart activity. The classic approach records the electrical signal using

(ECG). Electrodes placed on the chest pick up the electrical signal of each heartbeat, which can be described as a PQRST signal, where the distance between the R peaks (the R–R interval) gives the heart rate.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

# An idealised ECG: each wave is a Gaussian bump with a typical timing (s), width (s), and height (mV)
# relative to the R peak. Two beats 0.85 s apart give a heart rate of about 70 bpm.
waves = {"P": (-0.16, 0.025, 0.15), "Q": (-0.025, 0.008, -0.10), "R": (0.0, 0.010, 1.0),
         "S": (0.025, 0.008, -0.25), "T": (0.30, 0.050, 0.30)}
fs, r_times = 1000, [0.6, 1.45]
t = np.arange(0, 2.2, 1 / fs)
ecg = np.zeros_like(t)
for r in r_times:
    for centre, width, height in waves.values():
        ecg += height * np.exp(-((t - r - centre) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.plot(t, ecg, color="C0", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("Voltage (mV)")
ax.set_xlim(0.2, 2.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.85, 1.35)
r = r_times[0]
offsets = {"P": (0, 0.07), "Q": (-0.035, -0.02), "R": (0, 0.07), "S": (0.035, -0.02), "T": (0, 0.07)}   # label positions
for name, (centre, width, height) in waves.items():                 # label each wave of the first beat
    dx, dy = offsets[name]
    ax.annotate(name, (r + centre + dx, height + dy), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")

def bracket(x0, x1, y, label, below=True):
    """A horizontal bracket between x0 and x1 at height y, with a label."""
    tick = 0.04
    ax.plot([x0, x0, x1, x1], [y + tick, y, y, y + tick] if below else [y - tick, y, y, y - tick], color="0.3", lw=1)
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y - 0.02 if below else y + 0.03, label, ha="center", va="top" if below else "bottom", fontsize=9, color="0.3")

p_on, q_on, s_off, t_off = r - 0.21, r - 0.04, r + 0.045, r + 0.40
bracket(p_on, q_on, -0.34, "PR interval")
bracket(q_on, s_off, -0.34, "QRS")
bracket(q_on, t_off, -0.62, "QT interval")
bracket(r_times[0], r_times[1], 1.2, "R–R interval (heart rate = 60 / R–R)", below=False)
ax.set_title("An idealised ECG: the waves of one heartbeat and the intervals read from them")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure: An idealised ECG trace of two heartbeats, drawn from Gaussian bumps at typical timings. The P wave is the atria contracting, the QRS complex the ventricles contracting, and the T wave the ventricles recovering. The PR interval, the QRS width, and the QT interval are what a clinician reads; the R–R interval between beats is what music research mostly uses, since it gives the heart rate and its variability.
Many people now wear watches with built-in

(PPG), which measures heart rate using optical sensors. These are flexible, since they can measure at the wrist, finger or ear. But they are more sensitive to motion than ECG and less reliable for short-term HRV or spectral analyses. As a rule of thumb, use ECG when you need a clean, high-quality signal, and PPG when simple heart-rate tracking is enough.
You can try PPG with nothing but a phone. The

app reads the pulse from a fingertip pressed over the camera lens, or, more weakly, from the changing colour of the face in a webcam image, and shows the pulse wave, the heart rate, and a rough estimate of its variability. It also shows why the rule of thumb above holds: a moving finger or a change in the light breaks the signal at once.
The heart pumps around 7,500 litres per day for an average adult at rest.

Heart rate (HR) is conventionally reported in beats per minute (bpm). Typical resting adult HR is around 60–100 bpm (well-trained athletes commonly 40–60 bpm; infants and children are considerably higher), and HR can change by a few to several tens of bpm with arousal, movement or exercise. So it is worth recording a baseline heart rate and using within-participant normalisation to account for differences in resting HR and fitness.

Heart-rate variability (HRV) adds complementary information about autonomic balance. Because it varies so much with heart rate, always analyse it alongside respiration and/or motion data, so you can tell autonomic effects apart from metabolic or motor ones.

Heart rate is read off the time between successive R-peaks in the ECG. The variability of those intervals (HRV) carries autonomic information. Below we synthesise an ECG with realistic beat-to-beat variation, detect the peaks, and compute mean HR plus two common HRV measures, SDNN and RMSSD (roughly, the overall spread of the intervals and the typical size of beat-to-beat jumps).

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
fs = 250
n_beats = 40
rr = np.clip(1.0 + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n_beats), 0.6, 1.4)   # RR intervals (s)
peak_times = np.cumsum(rr)

t = np.arange(0, peak_times[-1] + 1.0, 1 / fs)
ecg = sum(np.exp(-((t - pt) ** 2) / (2 * 0.01 ** 2)) for pt in peak_times)
ecg += 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(len(t))

peaks, _ = find_peaks(ecg, height=0.5, distance=int(0.4 * fs))
rr_det = np.diff(t[peaks])
print(f"Detected {len(peaks)} beats | mean HR {60 / rr_det.mean():.1f} bpm")
print(f"SDNN {1000 * rr_det.std():.1f} ms | RMSSD {1000 * np.sqrt(np.mean(np.diff(rr_det) ** 2)):.1f} ms")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 4))
ax[0].plot(t, ecg, lw=0.6)
ax[0].plot(t[peaks], ecg[peaks], "rx")
ax[0].set_xlim(0, 6)
ax[0].set_title("Synthetic ECG with detected R-peaks (first 6 s)")
ax[0].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax[1].plot(t[peaks][1:], 60 / rr_det, "o-")
ax[1].set_title("Instantaneous heart rate")
ax[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax[1].set_ylabel("HR (bpm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

children.value: You can do a rough version of the studies described above with nothing but a clock.
Sit still for two minutes, then count your pulse for 30 seconds and double it. This is your baseline.
Listen to a calm, slow, quiet piece for three minutes. Count again, still seated.
Listen to something fast, loud, and driving for three minutes. Count again.

Write down the three numbers and answer: which direction did they move, and by how much? Then list at least three things other than the music that could have produced the same change. What would you have to control to turn this into a study rather than an anecdote?

is the record of how people breathe. The main variables to look at are breathing rate (breaths per minute), tidal depth (how big each breath is), the timing of inhalation versus exhalation, and instantaneous breathing phase (where in the breath cycle you are at any moment). Typical resting adult values: breathing rate ≈ 12–20 breaths/min, tidal volume ≈ 400–600 mL per breath, and an inspiratory:expiratory ratio around 1:2 (inspiration ≈ 1.5–2.0 s, expiration ≈ 2.5–3.5 s at ~12 bpm).
A common respiration device is the
, which gives precise measurements of air flow and volume. It requires a mouthpiece, though, so it is not very practical for musical purposes. A
(RIP) belt is more practical, as it fits around the chest. It captures respiration phase and timing well, but is less accurate for absolute lung volume.

Breathing can also be read from motion. A phone lying flat on the chest or belly records the rise and fall of each breath with its built-in accelerometer, and a webcam sees the same movement of the shoulders and chest. The

app uses either source to draw the breathing waveform, mark each breath, and estimate the rate, which is close to what a belt measures and far from what a spirometer measures: the movement of the chest, not the air that moves.

We have a large number of EQ02 LifeMonitor sensor vests from Equivital that measure respiration, heart rate, and accelerometry in one device.

Body temperature has not traditionally been studied much in music research. Some research groups can now capture it with sensor vests, though, so it is becoming possible to study it. Medical applications often measure temperature rectally or tympanically, but for musical purposes skin temperature is more relevant, and there the relative change matters more than the absolute value. Skin temperature also changes slowly, over seconds to minutes, so expect gradual trends rather than sharp, moment-to-moment peaks in response to musical events.
We have also started capturing body temperature with

. One benefit is that a single camera can cover a large group, such as a whole orchestra or audience. Since these cameras only record temperature, they also effectively anonymise the data. Until recently their resolution was too poor to be useful, but the latest cameras offer full HD resolution, which makes them far more useful for analysis.

, EDA) is a simple way to index sympathetic arousal. When people are surprised, excited, or stressed, sweat-gland activity changes and the skin conducts electricity differently. In recordings we separate a slow baseline level (skin conductance level, SCL) from quick event-linked peaks (
, SCRs). In music studies you typically expect SCR peaks after surprising or high-arousal moments, and SCL shifts when arousal stays elevated.

EDA is best captured from stable sites such as the palms, where the signal is strongest. The participant should sit still, because motion makes the signal noisy. It also helps to record and report the likely confounds—room temperature and humidity, skin hydration, electrode placement, movement, and relevant medications—and to correct statistically for multiple trials or comparisons where needed.
The simulated trace below is a toy skin-conductance signal for practising the tonic and phasic vocabulary, not a measurement: a slowly drifting level with short bursts on top.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import savgol_filter
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,

    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
t = np.linspace(0, 80, 8000)
tonic = 1.8 + 0.25 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 55.0)
phasic = np.zeros_like(t)
for centre in (14.0, 22.0, 38.0, 51.0, 67.0):
    phasic += 1.4 * np.exp(-((t - centre) ** 2) / 1.1)
noise = 0.06 * rng.standard_normal(len(t))
raw = tonic + phasic + noise
smooth = savgol_filter(raw, window_length=51, polyorder=3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.plot(t, raw, alpha=0.35, label="Simulated noisy trace")
ax.plot(t, smooth, lw=1.2, label="Smoothed")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Relative SC (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Pedagogical simulation only")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

(EMG) measures the tiny electrical signals produced by muscle activation, and is commonly used to track the timing and amplitude of motor events. In music research it helps separate motor activity (playing an instrument, singing, tapping, or expressive facial movements) from autonomic responses like heart rate or skin conductance.

Typical EMG recordings use surface bipolar electrodes placed on the skin over the muscle of interest. Raw EMG is noisy, so preprocessing matters, and you need to watch how motion influences the result. With good filtering, though, EMG yields meaningful data. A recording is only the start. The signals above differ in what they index, how fast they change, and how easily they are disturbed, and the same trace can be read in several ways. This section compares them and lists the mistakes that are easiest to make.
The table below compares the signals discussed above: what each one captures, how fast it varies, and its strengths and limitations.
Dig deeper: sampling rates for body signals
The column on signal content explains the sampling recommendations. The sampling theorem from the

chapter applies to body signals exactly as it does to audio: the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal. In practice, physiological recording often samples far above that minimum, since many analyses need precise event timing rather than just the waveform. Heartbeats arrive only about once per second, but locating each R peak to within a millisecond, which heart rate variability analysis requires, calls for ECG sampled at hundreds of hertz.

At RITMO, most of our studies compare heart rate (from ECG), respiration (from RIP belts), temperature (from belts or thermal cameras), and muscle activation (from EMG). We also always record these together with accelerometry and audio/video documentation, so that we can correct for contextual factors.

None of these signals are easy to work with. Each one takes a good deal of pre-processing and analysis before it yields meaningful results. The payoff is that we can learn a lot about how people experience sound and music, with signals that are at least easier to interpret than brain measurements.

Physiological traces are easy to misread. Movement—tapping, posture shifts, speech—contaminates PPG and adds noise to ECG. Poor electrode contact and temperature swings produce artefactual steps in skin conductance, and slow drift in peripheral temperature can track clothing, room ventilation, and vasoregulation as much as it tracks the music. Before interpreting phasic responses, then, prefer within-participant baselines, time-lock events to musical structure, and co-register movement or video where you can.

Consumer wearables—watches, rings, earbuds with heart-rate sensing—make ecological measurement easy, but they usually cannot substitute for research-grade ECG, belt-based respiration, or lab EDA when you need precise timing, validated HRV, or a stable tonic estimate. Treat their output as a source of trends and prompts, not as automatic ground truth.

Even “peripheral” sensing produces personal data, so ethics matters here. Use informed consent that states the purpose, storage, sharing and withdrawal terms; protect the files under your institution’s rules; and avoid diagnostic language about individuals based on a single session. Classroom demonstrations should be clear about their limits and should not single people out. A critical look: singing together, breathing together

children.value: When a Swedish choir study made the news, the headlines said that singing together makes the singers’ hearts beat as one, and the story has since been retold as proof that music bonds people at the level of the body. The study behind the headlines, by Björn Vickhoff and colleagues at the University of Gothenburg

, is worth reading for what it actually measured. The researchers asked a choir of fifteen singers to perform three tasks while their heart rate and respiration were recorded: humming a single note, singing a hymn, and chanting a slow mantra.
The result was that heart-rate variability came to share a common structure across singers, and it did so because the

told them when to breathe. Singing forces a long, controlled exhalation punctuated by short inhalations at phrase boundaries; because respiration modulates heart rate (respiratory sinus arrhythmia), a shared breathing pattern produces a shared cardiac pattern. The effect was strongest for the slow, regularly phrased mantra and weakest for the freely hummed tone.
It is worth being precise about what this shows and what it does not:
is that structured singing synchronises respiration, and through it, cardiac variability.
is mechanical and well understood, and it does not require any appeal to emotional bonding.
is that a correlation between bodies is not evidence of a feeling. Whether synchronised breathing
the sense of connection that choir singers report is a separate question, and one that this design cannot answer.
That gap—between a measurable physiological effect and the experience someone reports—is where most of the interesting work in this field happens, and where most overreaching claims are made.

Later work has taken the question into the concert hall. Finn Upham’s analyses of audience video show that perceivers’ bodies are shaped by the music even when they sit still, and that moments of musical silence produce a shared stilling of the whole audience
. Whether that shared stillness is felt as connection is, again, a separate question.
, and it is openly available if you want to see how such an experiment is reported.

Physiological measurement grounds emotional and aesthetic responses in the autonomic nervous system, through signals such as heart rate, HRV, electrodermal activity and breathing. The chapter placed those signals in an emotional frame: what emotions are, the difference between perceived and induced emotion, the valence–arousal plane, and the mechanisms through which music evokes feeling. Reading these signals well depends on baseline control, multimodal context, and careful interpretation when you link a body state to a musical experience. Lab-grade and consumer sensors answer different questions, and ethics and privacy apply even when the recording seems lightweight.
How do heart rate and heart rate variability reflect different aspects of autonomic regulation during music listening?
In the choir study of singing together, why did heart-rate variability come to share a common structure across singers, and what does the study show and not show about emotional bonding?
What is the difference between perceived and induced emotion, and why must a study state which one it measures?
Choose a track that moves you: where would you place it on the valence–arousal plane, and which of Juslin’s mechanisms best explains your reaction?
Why might consumer wearable heart-rate data support some research questions but not others (for example short-term HRV), and what ethical issues persist even for “low-risk” sensing?
